🧵 LLMs are powerful, but generating tokens one-by-one is painfully slow.

A new paper, “Unlocking Lossless Speedups in LLMs via Discrete Diffusion,” proposes Uno - a way to make autoregressive LLMs generate multiple tokens in parallel without changing the original model’s output distribution.

Here’s the idea 👇

1/ The problem

Standard LLMs are autoregressive (AR):

“The capital of France is”

→ “Paris”
→ next token
→ next token
→ next token...
Each token depends on the previous one, so generation is inherently sequential.
This becomes expensive for:
• long reasoning traces
• coding agents
• tool-using agents
• RL rollouts
• high-concurrency serving
The GPU often spends more time moving model weights/KV-cache data than doing useful computation.

2/ Speculative decoding helps - but has a cost

Traditional speculative decoding uses:
Small draft model → proposes tokens → large model verifies them
For example:
Draft model proposes:
“The Eiffel Tower is located in Paris”
The large model verifies the proposed sequence in parallel.

If the tokens are accepted, we get several tokens for roughly the cost of one verification step.

The catch?

You need a separate draft model, additional memory, another KV cache, and careful alignment between draft and target models.

3/ Uno asks a different question

What if we could make the same LLM act as both:

🧠 Verifier: original autoregressive model
⚡ Drafter: diffusion-based parallel generator

Instead of training a second draft model, Uno adds lightweight LoRA diffusion adapters to the existing LLM.

So the architecture becomes:

AR weights
→ preserve model quality

Diffusion weights
→ optimize generation speed

The two pathways share the same underlying model.

4/ How does the diffusion pathway work?

Imagine the model has already generated:

“The Eiffel Tower is”
Instead of predicting only:

“located”

the diffusion pathway tries to draft a whole block:

“located in Paris, France.”
These tokens are proposed in parallel.

The goal isn't for the diffusion model to be perfect.
It just needs to produce drafts that are close enough to what the AR model would generate.

5/ The clever part: AR verification

Uno then sends the draft through the original AR model.

Suppose the diffusion pathway proposes:

“located in Paris, France and was completed”

The AR verifier might accept:

“located in Paris, France”

and reject the rest.

Only the valid prefix is retained.

If something is rejected, the AR model samples the correct replacement.

This is why the authors call the acceleration lossless.

The original AR model remains the final authority.

6/ Ψ-Spec

The paper introduces Ψ-Spec, the sampler that combines:

Diffusion drafting + AR verification + rejection sampling

The diffusion model proposes multiple tokens simultaneously.

The AR model verifies them.

Because the verifier is still the original AR model, the sampling procedure preserves its target distribution.

7/ A simple example

Suppose the AR model would generate:

“Machine learning models learn patterns from data.”

Normally:

Step 1: Machine
Step 2: learning
Step 3: models
Step 4: learn
Step 5: patterns
...

Uno might draft:

“Machine learning models learn patterns”

in parallel.

The verifier checks the proposed tokens.

If all are valid, several tokens are emitted in one iteration.

So instead of:

1 token → verify → 1 token → verify → 1 token

we get:

multiple-token draft → verify → multiple accepted tokens

That is where the speedup comes from.

8/ Why LoRA?
The diffusion pathway uses lightweight LoRA adapters rather than another full model.
For the Qwen3-8B experiment, the adapters add only about 0.35B trainable parameters.
This is significantly smaller than the 1.05B-parameter DFlash drafter used as one of the baselines.

Uno also shares a KV cache between drafting and verification, reducing peak memory.
9/ Training is also interesting
The authors don't retrain the whole LLM.

They first train the normal AR model.

Then:

Freeze the AR weights

Add diffusion LoRA adapters

Corrupt token blocks using discrete diffusion

Train the adapters to reconstruct/draft the tokens

Encourage drafts that have high acceptance probability under the AR verifier

The paper uses Diffusion Consistency Distillation + Total Variation loss for this process.

10/ Why this matters

The diffusion adapters are essentially learning:

“How can I predict several tokens at once that the original AR model is likely to accept?”

So the expensive model doesn't need to change its behavior.

The additional parameters are dedicated almost entirely to making inference faster.

That separation of quality vs. speed is the core design idea.

11/ The results are impressive
For the Qwen-based UnoQwen model:

⚡ 5,733 tokens/sec system throughput

vs.

• EAGLE-3: 4,944 tok/s
• DFlash: 5,351 tok/s

At maximum batch size, UnoQwen reaches about 1.6× the throughput of the base AR model.
At batch size 1, it reaches about 2.5× speedup over the base model.
12/ It isn't just about batch size 1
This is an important point in the paper.
Many acceleration papers emphasize single-request latency.

But real-world agentic systems often have:

• multiple users
• parallel agents
• tool calls
• retries
• branching trajectories
• RL rollouts

So the authors measure both:

Per-request throughput

and

System throughput at high batch sizes.

Uno maintains its speed advantage across evaluated batch sizes.

13/ Uno vs diffusion LLMs

Conventional diffusion LLMs can generate tokens in parallel, but they often introduce a quality ↔ speed tradeoff because the underlying AR model is modified or replaced.

Uno takes a different approach:

AR model = quality

Diffusion adapter = speed
AR verifier = correctness

So the diffusion component doesn't have to become the final model.

It only needs to produce useful proposals.

14/ Uno can also accelerate RL

This may be one of the most practical applications.

RL training for LLMs requires huge numbers of rollouts.

If generation is faster, RL training becomes faster too.

The paper reports up to 40% end-to-end RL training speedup, particularly for mathematics and coding experts.

15/ The broader idea
The interesting conceptual takeaway isn't just “diffusion makes LLMs faster.”
It's:
Separate the model that defines the distribution from the mechanism used to sample from it efficiently.
The AR model defines:

“What should the model generate?”

The diffusion pathway learns:

“How can we propose several tokens at once?”

The verifier guarantees:

“Only outputs consistent with the AR distribution survive.”

16/ Why I think this is interesting

There are three different approaches to faster LLM inference:

Speculative decoding

→ separate draft model

Diffusion LLMs

→ parallel generation, but potentially lossy

Uno

→ diffusion-based drafting + original AR verification

The third approach tries to combine the best properties of both.

17/ The key numbers

📌 UnoQwen
• 8B base model
• +0.35B diffusion parameters
• ~5,733 tok/s system throughput
• ~1.6× faster than base AR at max batch
• ~2.5× faster at batch size 1
• lower peak memory than EAGLE-3/DFlash

And the full Uno model reports speedups of up to ~3×, with gains retained at high batch sizes.

18/ The one-sentence summary

Uno turns diffusion into a lightweight “parallel proposal engine” for an autoregressive LLM, while keeping the original AR model as the exact verifier.

That gives you:

⚡ parallel token generation
🧠 original model quality
✅ lossless verification
💾 fewer additional parameters
📈 better throughput
🚀 faster RL rollouts

This is a pretty compelling direction for making long-context and agentic LLM workloads cheaper and faster.

A 260M-parameter encoder just outperformed every evaluated visual document retriever below 800M parameters on ViDoRe v3, and it was trained from scratch with no pretrained vision tower.

The model is NeoMME, from a research team at H Company. Most visual document retrievers in the ColPali family repurpose a generative VLM as an encoder: a separately pretrained vision tower, a projection layer, and a causal LLM decoder. NeoMME drops all three.

Under the hood:

- Raw 32×32 RGB image patches pass through layer norm and a 2-layer MLP; text tokens pass through a factorized embedding. Both then share every layer of a single bidirectional Transformer. No vision encoder, no patch merging.
- Images keep their native aspect ratio at dynamic resolution, with a longest-side cap sampled between 1,024 and 2,048 pixels during training. A 2D rotary position scheme gives text diagonal coordinates and image patches row/column coordinates.
- 16,384-token context, enough for two 4K UHD pages. Most layers use sliding-window attention with half-windows alternating between 256 and 1,024 tokens; every sixth layer and the last are global. Grouped-query attention, QK normalization, squared-ReLU MLPs, and zero-initialized residual branches complete the stack.
- A custom 131K-vocabulary BPE tokenizer allows merges across word boundaries and emits 44% fewer tokens than ModernBERT across 14 languages.

Pretraining uses a masked discrete-diffusion objective over text: each segment draws a random corruption rate, masked tokens are predicted with image patches kept visible, and loss is computed only at masked positions. Multimodal segments use a minimum 30% corruption rate so the model cannot lean on text shortcuts. At 90% masking, keeping the image visible lifts masked-token accuracy by roughly 38 to 40 percentage points. There is no pixel-reconstruction target at all. Each run saw about 524B packed tokens on 16 or 32 H100s, optimized with NorMuon and AdamW.

For retrieval, one forward pass feeds two jointly trained heads: a 128-dimensional late-interaction head scored with MaxSim, and a mean-pooled dense head trained at Matryoshka widths. Joint training adds 1.4 nDCG@10 points to late-interaction over training it alone.

The numbers:

- ViDoRe v3: 0.523 nDCG@10 (260M) and 0.556 (800M). The 260M model lands within 0.2 points of ColQwen2.5 with 14× fewer parameters.
- Indexing: 51.3 pages/s at 2048×2048 on one L40S, about 2× ColModernVBERT at the same input size.
- Storage: hierarchical token pooling at factor 8 plus int8 queries and binary documents shrink a page embedding from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB, a 255× reduction, while retaining over 95% of retrieval quality.
- Query encoding: 21 ms on an L40S, 78 ms on a 128-core CPU host.

The authors are candid about limits: roughly 7× less text pretraining data than ModernBERT, no image-level objective (frozen natural-image features are weak), and text-only retrieval on BEIR trails dedicated text models.

I asked Astra to build a function that scores grammar in headlines for readability and human preference. This is for my news project. Basically a deterministic function to score how well or how awkwardly a certain news headline is phrased. 

I have thousands of headlines and articles, generated by GPT, Claude and my own finetuned models. It's easy enough getting pairwise LLM judgments for which generation is better. But for RL training I want a fast, deterministic function scoring each generation without having to do N^2 LLM judge comparisons (and other problems with a noisy online judge as RL reward).

I already have a pretty good scoring function, evolved over weeks or RL training and analysis. But It's not good at all at scoring "how readable is this headline."

"GPT-6 Astra Seizes No. 1 on Code Arena WebDev With 35 Point Lead Over Claude"

Pre-Astra models got stuck on headline length, simple patterns and regexps. They built long lists of bad phrases and cliches. That was helpful. 

But Astra is actually building me a headline grammar scorer from the ground up.

I gave it some parameters for success, as well as scored data and previous ranking code and notes. But I didn't have to tell it to:
* collect more data
* study which terms and phrases are useful to predict LLM judgements (overfit to the data)
* generalize the features, turning turn specific text to "<company> raises <money_amount>" from specific examples
* use spaCy to disassemble headlines to repeatable structures
* look at cases with same words / similar embeddings but the LLM judges prefer a particular word order (see below)

This is work I would have done manually 20 years ago. So yes Astra is very much like a colleague I would like to have.

Will this work? We'll find out tomorrow. But it's doing what I've long wanted an LLM to actually do. 

A thorough job.

Every once it a while it shows me what it's working on, including notes like this:

"• One useful distinction is now explicit: “Combine AI Providers into Virtual Models” differs from “Build Virtual Models From Any AI Provider.” The new
check records that supplier-versus-input wording, not headline length. The blind judge preferred the second wording, but I’m retaining contrary
judgments rather than treating every match as an error."

You can train a small language model from scratch—and actually understand the whole pipeline.

MiniMind is an open-source, educational LLM project that aims to make end-to-end model training reproducible on an individual GPU. Its README documents a roughly 64M-parameter model, with the headline experiment describing about 2 hours for the SFT stage on one NVIDIA 3090 and a corresponding low-cost GPU run.

The value is not just the tiny model. MiniMind exposes the learning path that bigger frameworks often hide: native PyTorch implementations for data cleaning, pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, LoRA, RLHF with DPO, RLAIF with PPO/GRPO/CISPO, tool use, agentic RL, adaptive thinking, and distillation. It also branches into vision, omni-modal, diffusion-language, and linear-model variants.

That makes it a rare “read the code, run the experiment, change the idea” project. You can follow how data becomes tokens, how a transformer is trained, how alignment changes behavior, and how tool calls or reasoning-oriented training fit into the picture—without treating the model as a black box.

The repo is useful for students, researchers, and engineers who want a compact laboratory for LLM mechanics. It includes training scripts, evaluation code, datasets, an English README, Hugging Face/ModelScope links, and an online MiniMind demo.

The project is Apache-2.0 licensed. The README is refreshingly explicit about what its time and cost figures mean, so the experiment can be interpreted as a reproducible teaching target—not a promise that every hardware setup will match it.

This paper tackles a huge blind spot in modern offline RL.

It asks an important question of why are we bloating actors with slow diffusion and flow-matching models when the critic is the one being discarded after training anyway?

In real-world robotics, taking multiple denoising steps per decision destroys control frequency.
 
They flip that tradeoff by shifting the architectural burden entirely to the training phase. 

Deepening MLP critics usually blows up in offline settings due to optimization collapse and bootstrap drift.

But they stabilize the critic using a residual MLP backbone, n-step bootstrap targets, and categorical cross-entropy.

Because the deep critic does the heavy lifting, their framework (LAC) lets a bare-bones deterministic actor match the performance of heavy generative baselines on OGBench.

They also deliver up to 4x lower inference latency in a single forward pass & no distillation tricks are required.

So i feel its a super important read for everyone in RL.

Read the full paper here: https://t.co/ENSxOQII40

Abraham Wald wrote eight memoranda at Columbia in 1943 about which parts of a bomber to armor and did not draw a single plane. The Center for Naval Analyses printed all eight as a monograph in July 1980.

The Statistical Research Group he wrote them inside had Milton Friedman, George Stigler, Jacob Wolfowitz, and a bench of thirty Hunter and Vassar women running the numbers. Two future Nobel laureates sat at the same table counting bullet holes on planes that came home.

Wald wrote out the calculation and told the Navy to armor the parts of the returning bombers that had no bullet holes.

The image every teacher points at, a bomber silhouette dotted in red where the fire went, is not in the memoranda. Somebody else drew it later and gave it his name. The mathematics is what he left behind, all text.

The CNA monograph is a free PDF.
